title: Job 40:15–24
context: The LORD continues his second speech by pointing Job to behemoth, which he made as well as Job. The creature eats grass like an ox, has great strength, a tail that moves like a cedar, bones like bronze and iron, and rests in the marsh under the lotus and the willows, unafraid even when the river surges. The LORD calls it the chief of the ways of God and asks who could capture it. The identity of behemoth is uncertain: it is commonly taken as the hippopotamus, sometimes as the elephant, and some interpreters see a symbolic or mythic creature representing chaotic power that only God masters. The Hebrew word is related to the ordinary word for beast and may mean something like the great beast. The text’s point does not depend on settling the identification: even the mightiest creature belongs to God, who made it and controls it, while Job cannot. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about God’s power over all creation.

verses.text: “See now behemoth, which I made as well as you. He eats grass as an ox.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD pointing Job to behemoth, which he made as well as Job. The creature’s identity is uncertain, but its maker is not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as Creator of both Job and the mighty beast. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the identification loosely, whether a hippopotamus, an elephant, or a symbolic creature.

verses.text: Look now, his strength is in his thighs. His force is in the muscles of his belly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD describing behemoth’s strength in its thighs and belly. Its power is a display of God’s handiwork.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the creature’s might as testimony to the Creator’s greater might. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s portrait of a creature Job cannot master.

verses.text: He moves his tail like a cedar. The sinews of his thighs are knit together.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see behemoth moving its tail like a cedar, with sinews knit together. The description is poetic and vivid.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the imagery emphasizing strength. Readers in both traditions commonly read the line as poetic description and avoid building creature theories on it.

verses.text: His bones are like tubes of bronze. His limbs are like bars of iron.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see behemoth’s bones like tubes of bronze and limbs like bars of iron. Its body seems unbreakable to human eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see poetic imagery of overwhelming strength. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing a creature beyond human power yet fully under God’s.

verses.text: He is the chief of the ways of God. He who made him gives him his sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see behemoth called the chief of the ways of God, with its maker giving it its sword. The mightiest creature is still God’s creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s supremacy over even the greatest of his works. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as placing all power under the Creator who made it.

verses.text: Surely the mountains produce food for him, where all the animals of the field play.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the mountains producing food for behemoth where the animals of the field play. God provides even for the mighty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s generous care across creation (compare Psalm 104:14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s provision.

verses.text: He lies under the lotus trees, in the covert of the reed, and the marsh.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see behemoth lying under the lotus trees in the reeds and marsh. Its strength is at rest in the place God gave it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s ordering of creatures and their habitats. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as description within the LORD’s speech.

verses.text: The lotuses cover him with their shade. The willows of the brook surround him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the lotuses shading behemoth and the willows of the brook surrounding it. The creature is at home in its world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s provision of shelter for his creatures. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s portrait of a world he governs.

verses.text: Behold, if a river overflows, he doesn’t tremble. He is confident, though the Jordan swells even to his mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see behemoth unafraid when the river overflows, confident even as the Jordan swells. Its calm reflects its strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a creature unshaken by forces that terrify humans. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as pointing to the greater power of the God who made it.

verses.text: Shall any take him when he is on the watch, or pierce through his nose with a snare?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether anyone could capture behemoth or pierce its nose with a snare. Job cannot master it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question underscoring human weakness before God’s creation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the description of Leviathan that follows.
